narrative: The model estimated a 53% probability that you will leave, meaning it sees your departure as slightly more likely than your staying; because the promotion decision used retention risk, that forecast led to denial. The strongest signal was that you reported other job opportunities. This was uncommon among employees predicted to stay—only about 23% had another opportunity—so it markedly increased the model’s concern that you may leave. Your overall experience also pushed in the same direction: with 11 or more years, you fall outside the typical stay-predicted profile, where only about 15% have that much experience, suggesting your profile is more mobile. By contrast, your six to ten years in the current organization worked in your favor, since roughly 35% of stay-predicted employees share that tenure, and it lowered the leave risk. Even so, those positive signals were not enough to offset the first two. Next, you and your manager should discuss whether the other opportunity is serious, what career path and promotion criteria would keep you engaged, and whether a retention-based promotion decision is fair given the model’s uncertainty. The organization should also review whether denying promotion solely because of a 53% leave forecast may itself increase your intention to leave.
